questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution: The blank describes the verb 'spread' in an 'as ___ as' comparison, so an **adverb** is needed: spread rumour as effectively as. Effective is an adjective, effectiveness a noun and effected a verb form.
questions.shortcut: Blank modifies a verb → -ly adverb.
questions.passage: Few inventions have spread rumour as (1) ___ as the forwarded message. A claim that once travelled by word of mouth, losing force at each retelling, now reaches thousands in minutes, often stripped of its source and (2) ___ with an urgent plea to 'share before it is deleted'. The trouble is not that people are foolish; it is that checking takes effort while forwarding takes a single tap. Researchers have found that a brief pause — even a prompt asking readers whether a headline is accurate — (3) ___ the sharing of false stories noticeably. Such nudges do not (4) ___ anyone's freedom to speak; they simply restore the moment of reflection that speed has erased. A society that learns to hesitate before it forwards will find that truth, which walks, has a fair chance of (5) ___ with lies, which run.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
questions.solution: The message loses its source but gains an urgent plea: it is **tagged with** the plea. Robbed, deprived and emptied take 'of' and describe losing something, which does not fit 'with an urgent plea'.
questions.shortcut: Preposition check: ___ with → tagged; robbed/deprived/emptied → of.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: Ignore the part between the dashes: the subject is 'a brief pause' (singular), and the that-clause needs a finite present verb → **curbs**. 'Curb' would need a plural subject; 'curbing' and 'to curb' are not finite verbs.
questions.shortcut: Remove the dash-interrupter, then match verb to subject.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution: The writer is answering a possible objection — that nudges limit free speech — so the verb means limit: nudges do not **curtail** freedom. 'Enhance' and 'celebrate' are not objections anyone would answer; 'express a freedom' is meaningless.
questions.shortcut: 'do not ___; they simply ___' — the first blank is the complaint being denied.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution: Truth 'walks' and lies 'run', so the real question is whether truth can **keep pace** (move at the same speed) with lies. Keeping quiet, keeping company and keeping faith do not continue the walking-running image.
questions.shortcut: Follow the image: walks vs runs → speed → pace.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

OSTENTATIOUS
questions.solution: Ostentatious means designed to impress others with wealth or display — **showy**. Modest is its antonym; secretive and thoughtful are unrelated.
questions.shortcut: ostentatious → 'ostent' = show off (think 'ostentation').

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

AMELIORATE
questions.solution: Ameliorate means to make a bad situation better (from Latin *melior*, better). Its antonym is **worsen**. Improve is the synonym trap; soothe is close in sense; tolerate is unrelated.
questions.shortcut: melior = better (French meilleur) → opposite = worsen.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To call a spade a spade
options: to work hard in the fields
to hide the truth behind polite words
to speak plainly and frankly, even if it is blunt
questions.solution: Calling a tool by its real name means **speaking plainly**, without softening the truth. The last option is the opposite; the field-work option is a literal reading; exaggeration is unrelated.
questions.shortcut: Naming things exactly = frank speech.

questions.q: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
questions.solution: The correct spelling is **occasion** — double c, single s. Acquaintance (acq-), guarantee (-ua-, -ee) and perseverance (no 'r' after the second e) are all correct.
questions.shortcut: occasion: two c's, one s (the reverse of 'necessary', which has one c, two s's).

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: **Surveillance** comes from French *surveiller* (sur + veiller, to watch over): s-u-r-v-e-i-l-l-a-n-c-e. Survelliance moves the i, Surveilance drops an l, Survaillance changes 'ei' to 'ai'.
questions.shortcut: sur + VEIL + lance: watch over something as if through a veil.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

A person who is indifferent to pleasure and pain
questions.solution: A **stoic** bears pleasure and pain alike without showing feeling. A cynic distrusts people's motives; a hedonist lives for pleasure; a sceptic doubts accepted beliefs.
questions.shortcut: Stoic = steady; hedonist = pleasure-seeker (opposites of each other).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The minister's speech was so ___ that even his critics were persuaded.
questions.solution: A speech that persuades even critics is **eloquent** (fluent and moving). Verbose means using too many words; taciturn means saying very little; incoherent means confused — none of these would persuade critics.
questions.shortcut: Result clause ('even critics were persuaded') decides the tone: positive.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The old building was pulled ___ to make way for a metro station.
questions.solution: **Pull down** = demolish, which is what clearing space for a station needs. Pull off = achieve something difficult; pull out = withdraw; pull over = stop a vehicle at the roadside.
questions.shortcut: Buildings are pulled down; plans are pulled off.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

Unless you do not work hard, (a) you will not (b) pass the examination (c) No error (d)
options: Unless you do not work hard,
questions.solution: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'do not' creates a double negative. Correct: '**Unless you work hard**, you will not pass the examination.'
questions.shortcut: Unless / until / lest never take another 'not'.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

He is one of those leaders (a) who has never (b) broken a promise (c) No error (d)
options: He is one of those leaders
questions.solution: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'leaders' (plural), not to 'one', so the verb must be plural: 'one of those leaders who **have** never broken a promise.'
questions.shortcut: one of those + plural noun + who → plural verb.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to replace the bold part of the sentence.

I would rather die **than to beg for mercy**.
questions.solution: 'Would rather' is followed by the bare infinitive on **both** sides: would rather die than **beg**. 'To beg' and 'begging' break the parallel, and 'but' cannot replace 'than' in this comparison.
questions.shortcut: would rather / had better → V1 (no 'to').

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Somebody must have stolen my purse.
options: My purse must have been stolen.
My purse must had been stolen.
questions.solution: Modal + have + V3 becomes **modal + have been + V3** in the passive; an indefinite agent (somebody) is dropped. 'Must had' is wrong after a modal, 'must have stolen' is active, and 'must be stolen' changes the time.
questions.shortcut: must have + V3 → must have been + V3; drop 'by somebody'.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "Alas! I have lost my wallet."
options: He exclaimed with sorrow that he has lost his wallet.
He said alas that he had lost his wallet.
He exclaimed with sorrow that I had lost my wallet.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his wallet.
questions.solution: 'Alas' is replaced by **exclaimed with sorrow**; present perfect goes back to past perfect (had lost); I/my become he/his. B misses the backshift; C keeps the interjection; D does not change the pronouns.
questions.shortcut: Interjection → 'exclaimed with joy/sorrow' + tense backshift.

questions.q:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph.

**A.** Within a decade, the terraces were green again and the village wells held water through the summer.
**B.** The villagers of a drought-hit hamlet once decided to stop waiting for rain and start catching it.
**C.** The success drew visitors from neighbouring districts, who went home to dig trenches of their own.
**D.** They dug contour trenches across the bare hillside and planted grass to hold the soil.
questions.solution: **B** introduces the villagers and their decision; **D** ('They dug...') is the action; **A** is the result a decade later; **C** ('The success...') refers back to that result. D cannot open because 'They' has no referent, and C cannot come before A because the success has not yet happened.
questions.shortcut: Opener has no pronoun (B); 'They' → D; 'The success' needs A before it.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Let's go for a walk, ___?
questions.solution: A sentence beginning with **Let's** (a suggestion that includes the speaker) always takes the tag **shall we?** The other tags are ordinary auxiliary tags and do not follow 'Let's'.
questions.shortcut: Let's → shall we?

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Translators are traitors who distort the works they translate.
A literal translation is always better than a free one.
Humour can never be translated from one language into another.
Translation always involves choosing what to keep and what to lose, and good translators succeed by making those choices go unnoticed.
questions.solution: The passage moves from 'nothing survives unchanged' to 'the translator must choose' to 'the best translators are invisible'. B is the jibe the author calls unfair; C is denied ('Neither approach is simply right'); D overstates 'may fall flat'.
questions.shortcut: Reject the option that repeats a view the author rejects (the jibe).
questions.passage:
Every translator knows the old Italian jibe that the translator is a traitor. The charge is unfair, but it contains a truth that readers rarely consider: no sentence survives the passage from one language to another unchanged. Words carry histories, sounds and associations that have no exact equivalents elsewhere. A Hindi speaker who calls a friend 'yaar' conveys an ease that 'friend' only approximates, and a pun that delights in one tongue may fall flat, or even offend, in another.

The translator must therefore choose, again and again, what to preserve and what to sacrifice. Some aim at fidelity to the letter, keeping the original's structure even when it sounds stiff; others aim at fidelity to the effect, rewriting freely so that the new reader laughs where the old reader laughed. Neither approach is simply right. A literal rendering of a legal contract is a virtue; a literal rendering of a comic poem may be a small crime.

What makes the work remarkable is that the best translators remain nearly invisible. When a translated novel reads as though it had been written in our own language, we praise the author and forget the person who made the book possible. Perhaps that is the final paradox of the craft: its highest success is to be overlooked, and the traitor's truest loyalty is shown in a thousand decisions that no reader ever notices.

questions.q: According to the passage, a literal rendering is a virtue in the case of —
questions.solution: 'A literal rendering of a legal contract is a virtue; a literal rendering of a comic poem may be a small crime.' The other options come from other parts of the passage but are not called virtues of literal translation.
questions.shortcut: Locate 'virtue' and read the noun it is attached to.

questions.q: The example of the word 'yaar' is used to show that —
options: friendship is valued more in India than elsewhere
some words carry shades of meaning that have no exact equivalent in another language
Hindi is a richer language than English
questions.solution: The example comes right after 'Words carry histories, sounds and associations that have no exact equivalents elsewhere' — 'friend' only **approximates** 'yaar'. The passage makes no claim that one language is richer, and makes no cultural or stylistic ruling.
questions.shortcut: An example proves the sentence just before it.

questions.q: The phrase 'a small crime' suggests that a literal translation of a comic poem —
options: would destroy the humour the poem was meant to create
would make the poem too long
questions.solution: The phrase is figurative. Comedy depends on effect ('the new reader laughs where the old reader laughed'), so a word-for-word version kills the joke — that is the 'crime'. There is no legal sense, length is never discussed, and 'impossible' is contradicted by the idea of 'may be'.
questions.shortcut: Figurative phrase → read it through the contrast (contract = letter, poem = effect).

questions.q: What is the 'final paradox' that the author refers to?
options: A translator must be disloyal to both languages at once.
A translator's greatest success lies in not being noticed.
Translators are praised more than the authors they translate.
The most accurate translations are always the least readable.
questions.solution: The next words explain it: 'its highest success is to be overlooked' — the better the translator, the less anyone notices. B reverses the passage ('we praise the author and forget the person'); C and D are not stated.
questions.shortcut: A 'paradox' is usually explained right after the colon — read it back.
